Three Uses of the Law
three YOO-sez uv thuh LAW
noun phrase
From the Latin usus legis (uses of the law), a technical Reformed and Lutheran distinction articulated by Calvin in the Institutes (II.vii) and by Melanchthon. The threefold classification systematizes what Scripture itself teaches about the law’s multiple functions in the life of mankind and the church.

See also: Three Uses of the Law

Biblical Definition

The doctrine of the three uses of the law teaches that God’s moral law—most fully expressed in the Ten Commandments—serves three distinct but related functions in its application to human beings. The first use (usus politicus or civilis) is the civil or political use: the law restrains gross outward wickedness in society by attaching punishments to violations, preserving civil order among the unregenerate (1 Tim. 1:9). The second use (usus elenchticus or paedagogicus) is the convicting or pedagogical use: the law reveals sin in its true guilt before God, driving the conscience to despair of self-righteousness and to flee to Christ for mercy (Rom. 3:20; Gal. 3:24). This is the law as schoolmaster leading to Christ. The third use (usus normativus or didacticus)—which Calvin and the Reformed tradition regard as the principal use—is the normative use for the regenerate: the law, received not as a covenant of works but as a rule of life, instructs the believer in what pleases God and directs his sanctification (Ps. 119:105; Rom. 7:22). Lutheranism historically emphasizes the second use; the Reformed tradition emphasizes the third. The 1689 Baptist Confession (19.6) and the Westminster Confession (19.6) affirm all three uses, insisting that while the law cannot justify the believer, it remains a binding guide for righteous living under grace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Law: a rule of action prescribed by authority; in theology, the declared will of God binding the creature and revealing both duty and the consequence of its violation.

expand to see more

LAW, noun. (Theology) The revealed will and command of God; that which He has enjoined upon His creatures as a rule of moral action—distinguishing the moral law (eternal and binding all persons), the ceremonial law (Levitical ordinances abrogated in Christ), and the judicial law (polity of Israel, expired with that commonwealth).

2. The Ten Commandments as the summary of the moral law, repeated and confirmed throughout Scripture as the standard of righteousness required of man.

3. (Use of the Law, Civil) That function of law by which gross sin is restrained in unregenerate society through the fear of punishment—the law as a curb or bridle on external wickedness.

4. (Use of the Law, Convicting) That function of law by which the conscience is convicted of sin and driven to seek mercy—the law as a mirror showing man his defilement.

5. (Use of the Law, Normative) That function of law by which the regenerate are directed in thankful obedience—the law as a lamp showing the path of life under grace.

Key Scripture

Galatians 3:24 — "Therefore the Law has become our tutor to lead us to Christ — so that we may be justified by faith."

Romans 3:20 — "Because by the works of the Law no flesh will be justified in His sight — for through the Law comes the knowledge of sin."

Romans 7:7 — "What shall we say then? Is the Law sin? May it never be! On the contrary, I would not have come to know sin except through the Law. For I would not have known about coveting if the Law had not said, 'You shall not covet.'"

Psalm 119:105 — "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path."

Modern Corruption

Antinomian strands in modern evangelicalism collapse the third use into the second, treating the law as purely convicting with no ongoing normative role for the believer—a position the Reformation confessions uniformly rejected.

expand to see more

Popular “grace-only” preaching, influenced by hyper-dispensationalism and therapeutic Christianity, treats any appeal to the law as a form of legalism that undercuts assurance and joy. This conflates the law as covenant of works (which Christ has ended for the believer) with the law as rule of life (which Christ upholds and writes on the regenerate heart). The result is what the Reformers called antinomianism—the practical abandonment of the law’s normative function, producing churches where sin is renamed, discipline atrophies, and the detailed guidance of God’s commands is replaced by vague appeals to love or the Spirit. Romans 7:22 (“I delight in the law of God after the inward man”) and Psalm 119 demolish this reading.

On the opposite extreme, moralist preaching collapses the second and third uses into the first—using the law primarily as a social-behavior code without first using it to slay self-righteousness and drive the hearer to Christ. Both errors produce churches without gospel: one substitutes sentiment for law, the other substitutes law for gospel. The confessional Reformed tradition holds the law and gospel in proper sequence: the law reveals sin, the gospel announces pardon in Christ, the law then guides the pardoned in the path of sanctification—each in its own place, neither displacing the other.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin usus captures the functional analysis: the same law, the same text, performing distinct God-appointed works on distinct hearers in distinct conditions.

expand to see more

Latin usus — use, function, application; the organizing term of the Reformed doctrine reflecting the law's context-sensitive operations

Latin politicus / civilis — civic, political; the first use that orders common life among the unregenerate through fear of punishment

Latin elenchticus — convicting, exposing; from Greek elegchein (to reprove, convict); the law as mirror showing sin's guilt

Latin paedagogicus — of a tutor or schoolmaster; Gal. 3:24’s image of the law as the teacher escorting pupils to Christ

Latin normativus / didacticus — normative, instructive; the principal Reformed use—the law as lamp directing the regenerate walk

Usage

"The second use of the law is the evangelistic use: any faithful sermon that aims at conversion must first use the law to show the hearer the full weight of his guilt before God, so that the gospel of free justification lands on a conscience that has been stripped of self-righteousness."

"The third use is the sanctification use: after justification, the believer loves the law (Ps. 119:97) not as a way of earning favor but as the revealed pattern of the life that pleases the God who has already declared him righteous in Christ."

"Lutheranism and Reformed theology historically part ways on whether the third use is the ‘principal’ use (Calvin's position, affirmed in the Westminster and 1689 Confessions) or whether the second use exhausts the law's theological function for the church."
